h.select_rule: Discard any hypothesis whose condition is the edited field's own current value, or whose condition merely disables or disconnects the edited component. From the rest, keep 10 with distinct mechanisms and field pairs, favouring those where an informed expert could plausibly bet on either direction.
h.strategy: Two patterns are banned because experts find them obvious: (1) conditioning on the current value of the same field being edited, which just restates that upgrading a weak setting helps more than upgrading a strong one; (2) conditions that make the edited component unused, unreachable or inert. Instead, each hypothesis must link two DIFFERENT fields that interact through a non-trivial mechanism, such as substitution between parallel routes, a capacity already supplied elsewhere, one part acting as a bottleneck for another, or interference that turns a usually helpful edit harmful. No condition setting may appear in more than two hypotheses. Use the gaps and negated assumptions as the source of each idea. In each 'why', name the mechanism and explain why the opposite direction is also a priori plausible.

hyps.why: The L2 term is normalized by batch size, so a larger batch dilutes the effective penalty and relieves over-regularization exactly when alpha is high.
Under standard parameterization wider nets change their function more per step, so widening at already-unstable LRs aggravates divergence.
A strong L2 penalty shrinks every layer, and the shrinkage compounds multiplicatively through an added layer, worsening underfitting.
At unstable learning rates, fewer and less noisy updates per epoch partially rescue training, so increasing batch size helps most there.
Large batches give few updates in 243 epochs plus cleaner gradients, so a higher LR both compensates for the step deficit and stays stable.
Deep ReLU stacks amplify update magnitudes through layer products, so raising LR triggers divergence or dead units sooner than in shallow nets.
Narrow layers act as information bottlenecks and lose units to dead ReLUs, which each additional layer compounds.
Wide standard-parameterized nets hit the instability threshold at smaller LRs, so increasing LR hurts them more than narrow nets.
Large batches give few updates and narrow nets fit more slowly per step, so shrinking width compounds undertraining.
Extra depth is only exploitable when LR is neither too low to train it nor too high to keep it stable, so it pays off mainly at mid LR.
